\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{अश्वत्थः} (aśvatthaḥ)}{अश्वत्थः (aśvatthaḥ)}]{\sk{अश्वत्थः} (aśvatthaḥ) — a sacred fig tree}

\label{lesson:SA-C166-asvatthah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a live coal, then the Sanskrit for iron.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अश्वत्थः}}
\textbf{\sk{अश्वत्थः}} — \emph{aśvatthaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a sacred fig tree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aśvattha} \textquotedblleft{}the sacred fig tree\textquotedblright{} has a disputed origin: MW reads it as \emph{aśva} \textquotedblleft{}horse\textquotedblright{} + \emph{-stha} \textquotedblleft{}standing\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}the tree horses stand under\textquotedblright{}, but CDIAL 922 reports Mayrhofer's view that it is non-Aryan and unconnected with \emph{aśva}. It is old, in the Atharvaveda.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{निम्बः} (nimbaḥ)}{निम्बः (nimbaḥ)}]{\sk{निम्बः} (nimbaḥ) — a neem tree}

\label{lesson:SA-C166-nimbah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for iron, then the Sanskrit for a sacred fig tree.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{निम्बः}}
\textbf{\sk{निम्बः}} — \emph{nimbaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a neem tree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nimba} \textquotedblleft{}the neem tree\textquotedblright{} appears in the ritual manuals, and neither MW nor CDIAL 7245 gives a derivation, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi \emph{nīm} and Punjabi \emph{nimb} (CDIAL 7245).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{आम्रवृक्षः} (āmravṛkṣaḥ)}{आम्रवृक्षः (āmravṛkṣaḥ)}]{\sk{आम्रवृक्षः} (āmravṛkṣaḥ) — a mango tree}

\label{lesson:SA-C166-amravrksah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a sacred fig tree, then the Sanskrit for a neem tree.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{आम्रवृक्षः}}
\textbf{\sk{आम्रवृक्षः}} — \emph{āmravṛkṣaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a mango tree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{āmravṛkṣa} is built from \emph{āmra} \textquotedblleft{}mango\textquotedblright{} and \emph{vṛkṣa} \textquotedblleft{}tree\textquotedblright{} (MW). Neither MW nor CDIAL gives a derivation for \emph{āmra}, so its origin is uncertain; it lives on as Hindi \emph{ām} \textquotedblleft{}mango\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 1268).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वटः} (vaṭaḥ)}{वटः (vaṭaḥ)}]{\sk{वटः} (vaṭaḥ) — a banyan tree}

\label{lesson:SA-C166-vatah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a neem tree, then the Sanskrit for a mango tree.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वटः}}
\textbf{\sk{वटः}} — \emph{vaṭaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a banyan tree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vaṭa} \textquotedblleft{}the banyan\textquotedblright{} appears from the Mahābhārata on. MW thinks it perhaps a Prakrit form of \emph{vṛta} \textquotedblleft{}surrounded, covered\textquotedblright{}, but marks that as a guess, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi \emph{baṛ} \textquotedblleft{}banyan\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11211).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{तालः} (tālaḥ)}{तालः (tālaḥ)}]{\sk{तालः} (tālaḥ) — a palm tree}

\label{lesson:SA-C166-talah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a mango tree, then the Sanskrit for a banyan tree.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तालः}}
\textbf{\sk{तालः}} — \emph{tālaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a palm tree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tāla} \textquotedblleft{}the palmyra, the fan-palm\textquotedblright{} appears from Manu on (CDIAL 5750). DEDR 3180 sets it beside Dravidian words for the palm, noting that some of those may be borrowed from Indo-Aryan, so the direction is not settled. Punjabi kept it as \emph{tāṛ} \textquotedblleft{}fan-palm\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5750).
\end{cousinweb}
